[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Greedy Algorithms and Proof Strategies"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Greedy algorithms build a solution piece by piece, always choosing the next piece that offers the most immediate benefit. While they are efficient and intuitive, proving their correctness requires rigorous mathematical reasoning, typically via Greedy Choice Property or Optimal Substructure."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Core Concepts of Greedy Algorithms"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Greedy Choice Property: A globally optimal solution can be arrived at by making a locally optimal (greedy) choice."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Optimal Substructure: An optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems."},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Standard Proof Strategies"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Exchange Argument (Greedy Stays Ahead): Prove that if you take an optimal solution and swap its first choice with the greedy choice, the resulting solution remains valid and at least as good."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Proof by Induction: Show that the greedy choice works for the base case, and assuming it works for k steps, prove it holds for k + 1 steps."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Example: Activity Selection Problem"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Given a set of activities with start and finish times, select the maximum number of activities that can be performed by a single person, assuming that a person can only work on a single activity at a time. The greedy strategy is to always pick the activity that finishes earliest."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"def select_activities(start, finish):
    n = len(finish)
    selected = [0]
    i = 0
    for j in range(1, n):
        if start[j] >= finish[i]:
            selected.append(j)
            i = j
    return selected"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"By sorting the activities by their finish times in ascending order, the algorithm iterates through and greedily picks the next compatible activity, ensuring maximum remaining time for subsequent tasks."}]
